extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, War Department officials, and practitioners of military/admin law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and administrative rules governing appointment, muster, dismissal, status, and records of officers (Regular and Volunteer), including summary dismissal, board procedures, muster-in requirements, and the War Department's practice on official records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between summary dismissal and dismissal by sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary dismissals (e.g., to summarily rid the service of unworthy officers or by discharge/muster-out) are distinct from dismissal by sentence of court-martial; summary action has been repeatedly ordered even where court-martial previously acquitted the officer of the same offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat summary dismissals as an administrative/Executive power distinct in nature from judicial/military-sentenced dismissals; consult precedents (R. 23, 265; 26, 5; etc.) when assessing validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boards under section 14 (April 22, 1898) need not be sworn or record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A board appointed under section 14 of the act of April 22, 1898 to provide for temporarily increasing the military establishment is not required by statute or regulation to be sworn or to record evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These boards are summary proceedings adapted to wartime and may be regarded as in aid of the President's power to dismiss without trial; unlike earlier boards (act of July 15, 1870) they need not be sworn or keep evidentiary reports. Precedents: C. 4842 (Aug. 1898).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of summary dismissal requires delivery or official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary dismissal of an officer does not properly take effect until the order of dismissal or an official copy is delivered to him, or he is otherwise officially notified of the fact of the dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite P.49, 91, and 176 (Sept. 1891); C.4842 (Feb. 2, 1900); 16823 (Sept. 13, 1904). Absent delivery/notice, the dismissal is not operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: President may fix a future effective date for dismissal; acts valid until notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, when dismissing an officer by order, may fix a date in futuro when the discharge shall become operative; until the officer receives notice of the order, all his acts are legal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a future effective date is fixed, the War Department cannot make the discharge effective as of an earlier date. All official acts by the officer prior to notice are valid. (C.16823, Sept.13, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal 'by order of the Secretary of War' is legally act of the President
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary dismissal 'by order of the Secretary of War' is in law the act of the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite R.5, 319 (Nov. 1863); P.36, 322 (Nov. 1889); O.15973 (Mar.1, 1904). Treat such orders as Presidential acts for legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field commanders/dept commanders cannot summarily dismiss officers
rubrics_metrics.description: A department or Army commander has no authority to summarily dismiss or discharge an officer from the military service (subject to historical exceptions where later ratified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents disallow such authority (R.11, 405; 16, 553; 41,84; 42,263); exceptions occurred in Civil War where President later treated office as vacant and filled by appointment, thereby making the dismissal his own act.

rubrics_metrics.name: No revocation of a legally executed order of dismissal; finality of executed dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no revocation of a legally executed order of dismissal; the original dismissal is an act done which cannot be undone and the order evidencing it is incapable of revocation or recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An officer once legally separated can only be restored by a new appointment under the Constitution; indirect means (allowing resignation/retirement/honorable discharge) cannot legally restore him. (Multiple authorities cited: R.31,504; C.4586; O.4953; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Void revoking orders and de facto officer doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: An order assuming to revoke an executed legal order or sentence of dismissal is void and inoperative, but if the dismissed officer enters upon duties under the void order, he is a de facto officer vis-à-vis third parties; forged revoking orders can render the officer indebted for pay drawn as a de facto officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases C.691; 3735; 15973; O.9121 (forged order). Use de facto doctrine to protect third-party rights but not to restore legal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary discharge is a discharge without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary discharge of an officer is a discharge without honor in the same manner as the summary discharge of an enlisted man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: P.52,403 (Mar.21,1892); 60,250 (June 30, 1893); C.1789 (Oct.18,1895). Treat summary dismissals as dishonorable for record/status purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive dismissal does not disqualify for reappointment or civil office
rubrics_metrics.description: A dismissal of an officer by executive order does not operate to disqualify him for reappointment to military office or for appointment to civil office under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: R.36,330 (Mar.1875). Despite prior dismissal, reappointment or civil appointment is legally permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's authority to dismiss cadets without court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has authority to dismiss cadets from the United States Military Academy without trial by court-martial for cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority cited: C.10513 (May 20, 1901). Use Presidential dismissal power for cadets absent requirement of court-martial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Once notice served, President cannot revoke or pardon to restore cadet status
rubrics_metrics.description: After notice of dismissal has been served on cadets, the President is without power to restrict or revoke the dismissal order or to pardon so as to restore them to former status at the Military Academy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.25471 (Aug.24,1909). Once effective notice, restoration requires new appointment or other legal means, not mere revocation/pardon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary dismissal of a cadet is discharge without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary dismissal of a cadet is a discharge without honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: C.2533 (Aug.17,1896). Same dishonorable characterization as other summary dismissals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion subject to examination: failure causes reversion and suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer promoted subject to examination fails the exam for reasons other than physical, upon approval of the adverse findings he reverts to prior grade and enters upon any statutory suspension required in that lower grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: promoted first lieutenant to captain subject to exam; on failure reverted to first lieutenant and served suspension per act of Oct.1,1890. (C.23096, May25,1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail to other duties does not relieve primary battalion roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailing a battalion adjutant or quartermaster to duty elsewhere (e.g., with chief of police or school of musketry) does not relieve him of his battalion duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such details as temporary assignments; the officer retains primary status and responsibilities (C.16906; C.28998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power to prescribe volunteer appointment/promotion rules absent statute
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of statutory regulation, the Executive has power to prescribe rules governing appointment and promotion of officers of the volunteer forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.12599 (May 9, 1902). Use Executive regulations when Congress silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal acceptance is essential to complete appointment and start service
rubrics_metrics.description: The date on which a volunteer officer appointed by the President formally accepts his appointment should be considered the commencement date of his military service; prior service does not count under that appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.6644 (June,1899). Do not attribute service under an appointment before formal acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioning required for officers of U.S. Volunteers to hold office
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioned officers of United States Volunteers did not hold office until they were commissioned; remedial legislation recognizing pay prior to commissioning is only a recognition of the fact they were not in service during that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.7050 (Sept.1899 & Oct.1900); legislative remedies may be required to make payments for service before commissioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muster-in required for governors' appointees to vest office; appointment revocable until muster
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers of Volunteers appointed by governors under July 22, 1861 and similar acts did not fully vest until formally mustered in by a duly authorized mustering officer representing the United States; until muster-in the appointment was revocable by the governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.14587 (Jan.12,1904); C.9773 (Feb.26,1901). Mustering-in is essential to complete the federal acceptance and to fix tenure under federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mustering officers cannot backdate muster-in or recognize earlier grade date
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department will not recognize a mustering officer's acts to muster in an officer on one date but date his service from an earlier date, nor recognize grade/date conferred as of an earlier date than the muster roll states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.9773 (Feb.26,1901). Administrative acts cannot retroactively change official dates of commission or grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defective title by non-mustered officers; lawful acts valid for third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers who served and were treated contemporaneously as though in office but were not mustered in do not acquire rights based on defective title, but their lawful acts within apparent authority are valid and binding as to third persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.9773 (Feb.26,1901). Protect third-party transactions while distinguishing personal rights/claims based on legal title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of a new office vacates prior office
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance by an officer of a different office (e.g., captain of volunteers accepted assistant quartermaster of Volunteers) vacated his previous office (e.g., captain of Cavalry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.40,158 (Apr.1890). Acceptance is treated as resignation/abandonment of prior position for vacancy purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment/return to private status vacates previously held commission
rubrics_metrics.description: An enlisted man appointed and accepting a commission who, upon an order purporting to revoke his appointment, returns to service as a private as directed, thereby abandons the office and vacates it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.2293 (June 2,1896). An officer's conduct in acquiescing to demotion can create vacancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's dismissal power over volunteers differs from regular officers; cancellation of muster-in permissible for unfitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because volunteer officers serve for fixed limited terms, the President does not have the same power of dismissal as for regular officers; however, cancellation of a muster-in due to unfitness is a legal exercise of summary dismissal for cause vested by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Sec.17 of July 17, 1862 and authorities P.46,102; 52,496; 61,264. Use statutory dismissal powers applicable to volunteers rather than assuming identical authority as over regular officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil office generally not vacated by accepting Volunteer commission; exceptions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the government does not require complete severance from civil life for volunteers, a civil officer does not vacate such civil office by accepting and holding a commission in the Volunteer Army; however, acceptance after muster-in of the position of a member of the State legislature would vacate that civil office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.4223 (June 1,1898) and C.4233 (June 2,1898). Check specific statutes or rules for particular civil offices (e.g., state legislature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative acts preserving Regular commissions when taking Volunteer commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of Congress (May 28, 1898; Mar. 2, 1899) provided that Regular Army officers receiving Volunteer commissions should not be held to vacate their Regular Army offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.16823 (Sept.13,1904). Use these statutes to interpret concurrent holding of Regular and Volunteer commissions for officers already in Regular commission at time of Volunteer organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment to Regular Army under 1901 act does not per se vacate Volunteer commission
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of Volunteers appointed to office in the Regular Army under the act of Feb.2,1901 and amendments may lawfully continue to hold his Volunteer commission and exercise related functions; the Volunteer office is not vacated merely due to appointment to the Regular Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.16823 (Sept.13,1904). Distinguish between appointments and vacancies; statutory text governs interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolishment of an office converts status to civilian; dismissal rules do not apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The abolishment of an office through operation of law changes the occupant's status from officer to civilian; the rules governing dismissal of an office that continues to exist do not apply to abolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: supernumerary second lieutenant whose office abolished by act of Mar.3,1863 became civilian on approval date. (P.53,452; C.23071; I4148.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial sentence not effective until communicated; pending publication sentence may be without force
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence by general court-martial that is not shown to have been communicated to the officer and during which the officer was returned to duty 'without prejudice to sentence' may not be carried into effect prior to muster-out and thus be without force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sentence cashiered published in orders but not communicated; held sentence not effective prior to muster-out. (P.37,407 Jan.6,1890.) Ensure communication to officer before enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official War Department papers are confidential archives; copies furnished only by Secretary's authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Official papers on file in the War Department are not public records open to inspection; copies or consultation may be permitted only by the Secretary of War's authority, except where law or usage provides for furnishing or courts require production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish permanent records (general/special orders, muster rolls, discharges, commissions) from privileged communications (reports to superiors) which courts generally hold incompetent and refuse production. (R.19,375; C.7912.) Secretary should consider nature of information and proposed use when deciding.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department practice to decline furnishing copies except for Congress/courts/other executive uses
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the established practice of the War Department to decline to furnish copies of records except upon call from Congress/committees, order of United States court, or request from another executive branch for official use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.7912 (Oct.5,1910); C.2684-1 (June1,1910). The Secretary should weigh the private interests and public considerations; requests from Members of Congress for private legislative assistance may be declined.
